THOUGHT: The child has early-onset, recurrent, suppurative skin infections, recurrent fevers, lymphadenopathy, respiratory infections, and failure to thrive — a pattern typical of an innate immune defect affecting neutrophil microbicidal function. The leukocytosis with left shift supports ongoing bacterial infections. The key laboratory finding is an abnormal nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test and decreased neutrophil oxidative burst activity, which directly indicate defective NADPH oxidase function in phagocytes. This defect causes inability to generate reactive oxygen species needed to kill certain bacteria and fungi, leading to recurrent abscesses and infections (classically with catalase-positive organisms) beginning in infancy. Other diagnoses (e.g., leukocyte adhesion deficiency, severe congenital neutropenia, hyper-IgE, Chediak–Higashi) are less consistent with the abnormal NBT/decreased oxidative burst and the clinical picture. The most likely unifying diagnosis is therefore an X-linked (most common) chronic granulomatous disease due to NADPH oxidase deficiency.

DIAGNOSIS: Chronic granulomatous disease (most likely X‑linked NADPH oxidase deficiency).
